blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the Snowflake cloud-based data warehouse, highlighting its design as a disaggregated system where compute and storage are decoupled, enabling independent scaling and elasticity. He notes that while Snowflake excels in high-level cloud-native principles like disaggregation and isolation, challenges remain in fine-grained resource allocation and prediction of intermediate data volumes during query processing. The paper emphasizes how modern cloud infrastructure changes traditional assumptions in data warehouse design, particularly the need for elastic, fine-grained resource management. Colyer also points out Snowflake's three-tier ephemeral storage system for intermediate data, which is not fully disaggregated, and discusses the trade-offs in caching and elasticity, including the potential for future improvements like auto-scaling and serverless platforms.
paper_title: Building an elastic query engine on disaggregated storage
paper_abstract: We present operational experience running Snowflake, a cloudbased data warehousing system with SQL support similar to state-of-the-art databases. Snowflake design is motivated by three goals: (1) compute and storage elasticity; (2) support for multi-tenancy; and, (3) high performance. Over the last few years, Snowflake has grown to serve thousands of customers executing millions of queries on petabytes of data every day. This paper presents Snowflake design and implementation, along with a discussion on how recent changes in cloud infrastructure (emerging hardware, fine-grained billing, etc.) have altered the many assumptions that guided the design and optimization of Snowflake system. Using data collected from various components of our system during execution of 70 million queries over a 14 day period, our study both deepens the understanding of existing problems and highlights new research challenges along a multitude of dimensions including design of storage systems and high-performance query execution engines.
